monoclonal_antibodies.abstract: Abstract Multi-agent-based simulations (MABS) of electric vehicle (EV) home charging ecosystems generate large, complex, and stochastic time-series datasets that capture interactions between households, grid infrastructure, and energy markets. These interactions can lead to unexpected system-level events, such as transformer overloads or consumer dissatisfaction, that are difficult to detect and explain through static post-processing. This paper presents a modular, Python-based dashboard framework—built using Dash by Plotly—that enables efficient, multi-level exploration and root-cause analysis of emergent behavior in MABS outputs. The system features three coordinated views (System Overview, System Analysis, and Consumer Analysis), each offering high-resolution visualizations such as time-series plots, spatial heatmaps, and agent-specific drill-down tools. A case study simulating full EV adoption with smart charging in a Danish residential network demonstrates how the dashboard supports rapid identification and contextual explanation of anomalies, including clustered transformer overloads and time-dependent charging failures. The framework facilitates actionable insight generation for researchers and distribution system operators, and its architecture is adaptable to other distributed energy resources and complex energy systems. Computer Science > Computation and Language arXiv:2610.26474 (cs) [Submitted on 19 Oct 2026] Title: AfriGuard: Safety and Robust Refusal For African Languages Authors: Israel Abebe Azime , Jesujoba O. Alabi , Iffat Maab , Alexander D. Cai , Tadesse Destaw Belay , Atnafu Lambebo Tonja , Jonas Kgomo , Folasade Alabi , Salomey Osei , Saminu Muhammad Aliyu , Nkechinyere Faith Aguobi , Bontu Fufa Balcha , Blessing Sibanda , Davis David , Mouhamadane Mboup , Daud Abolade , Neo Putini , Louis Powell , Kiant'e Brantley , Philipp Slusallek , Dietrich Klakow , Julia Kreutzer View a PDF of the paper titled AfriGuard: Safety and Robust Refusal For African Languages, by Israel Abebe Azime and 21 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) designed to interact with users are typically trained to respond appropriately to harmful or toxic content. However, ensuring appropriate responses becomes more challenging in diverse linguistic and cultural contexts, where safety risks may be expressed or interpreted differently. Building safe AI systems therefore requires detecting safety risks, understanding their nature, and responding appropriately, while accounting for linguistic and cultural variations that add complexity to each stage. In this work, we introduce AfriGuard, a culturally grounded multilingual dataset for studying harmful intent, safety-category understanding, and refusal behavior across 10 African languages and English. Our findings reveal that guardrail models underperform both open- and closed-source LLMs on safety-intent and safety-category classification, while models show limited understanding of appropriate safety behavior, scoring below 60% F1. We further find that models often fail to respond appropriately to unsafe prompts not because they explicitly refuse, but because they produce linguistically inadequate responses that result in incidental non-assistance rather than proper refusals. Finally, using AfriGuard, we develop efficient guardrail models that achieve performance competitive with models up to 30x larger, introduce refusal detectors that improve average performance by 43.9% over existing detectors, and demonstrate that supervised fine-tuning can substantially improve overall safety performance. Quantitative Biology > Biomolecules arXiv:2610.30039 (q-bio) [Submitted on 21 Oct 2026] Title: Unlocking the Full Potential of Taylor Dispersion Analysis Through Advanced Detection Authors: Rami Laoufi (TechSep), Agnès Hagège (TechSep) View a PDF of the paper titled Unlocking the Full Potential of Taylor Dispersion Analysis Through Advanced Detection, by Rami Laoufi (TechSep) and 1 other authors View PDF Abstract: Today, pharmaceutical sciences rely on a wide range of innovative therapeutics of varying sizes: nanoparticles, proteins, antibodies, and nanocarriers for drug delivery. Measuring their size is one of the crucial parameters in their characterization, to ensure drug safety, stability, and effectiveness. Over the past two decades, Taylor Dispersion Analysis has emerged as an important sizing method. Its scope of application is perfectly suited to the sizes of these therapeutics. By design, it can be coupled with a wide range of detectors, and extensive research has been conducted in this field. In this review, we will present an overview of the studies conducted, and discuss how the application drives the choice of one detector or another (size measurement, aggregation studies, interaction studies, and other analyses, performed in both simple biological buffers and in more complex media, particularly serum) and makes Taylor Dispersion Analysis a highly versatile tool.
